questiontext.text:
Which is the best summary of the proof above that no route crosses each of the seven bridges of Königsberg exactly once?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A good summary names the method and the key step. Euler supposed that such a route exists, which is the start of a proof by contradiction. He wrote the route as a list of areas: 8 letters for 7 bridges. Then he counted how often each area must appear in the list, from the number of bridges at it: \(3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9\). The two counts disagree, so no such route exists. The best summary is the second.

The other summaries fail. Euler did not list routes: the counting argument shows that no route can exist without listing any. An odd number of bridges is not the obstacle: two areas joined by five bridges have a route. And five bridges at one area is no problem on its own: a route can start or end there and use all five. The contradiction comes from adding up the counts for all four areas.

questionvariables.text: ta1: [[k_try, false, "Euler listed every possible route through the town and checked each one, and found that none of them crossed all seven bridges exactly once."], [k_count, true, "Suppose there is such a route. Its list of areas would have 8 letters, one more than the number of bridges, but counting the bridges at each area shows that the list needs 9."], [k_odd, false, "Seven is an odd number, and a route that crosses every bridge exactly once is only possible when the number of bridges is even."], [k_five, false, "Area A has five bridges, which is too many: a route that reaches A by one bridge must leave by another, so one of A's bridges is left over."]];

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 8.8 (pp. 42-44) in Section 8 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: Yes: it names the method (suppose that a route exists) and the mechanism (count the letters in two ways).
Euler did not list routes. Counting shows that no route can exist without listing any.
